#1020. Sisters in Sweat: how a former Spurs player got 20,000 Indian women into sport

A dinner-party question, a Sunday kickabout and an idea that snowballed. Nine years on, Tanvie Hans and Swetha Subbiah have taken sporting sisterhood to 10 cities

On a breezy evening in 2017, as conversations flowed and so did the drinks at a dinner party, Tanvie Hans was asked an all-too-familiar question at the table: “Hey, can you teach me how to play football?”

For the Indian-born British footballer, who played professionally in England, it was an easy yes.

After a little planning and some back-and-forth messages 17 women – mostly friends and acquaintances – turned up for Hans’ first football lesson on a Sunday morning in the southern Indian metropolis of Bengaluru, eager to discover the joy of the sport.

Nine years on from that impromptu football session, the group has grown into a community of 20,000 women across India. They may not be sisters by blood, but they are the Sisters in Sweat. Co-founded by Hans and the performance coach Swetha Subbiah, Sisters in Sweat is India’s largest women-first sports community, built to help women move more, play more and connect through a variety of sports.

From Chandigarh in the north to Chennai in the south, the initiative now spans 10 Indian cities, with football among its most popular offerings. “It wasn’t something that Swetha and I sat down to plan or even recognised was a gap in the market,” Hans, a former Tottenham and Fulham midfielder, tells Moving the Goalposts.

“But the moment we started these sessions they became successful and the community kept growing organically. That’s when we recognised that we were catering to an audience that is not being catered to in this way. And who better to do it than two women who are experts in the field?”

At Sisters in Sweat, coach-led football sessions are conducted two to three times a week, with participants free to choose between beginner and intermediate sessions, depending on their level of ability. The entry fee starts at about 300 Indian rupees – just under £2.50 – and women of all ages are welcome. You could be trying football for the first time, getting back to it or simply looking for a fun way to stay active.

The format is pretty simple, and the same one Hans and Subbiah used at their first gathering in 2017. The session begins with a quick huddle; everyone introduces themselves and the coach explains what to expect in the next 90 minutes. A warm-up follows before partner or group drills help break the ice within the group, which often features new faces every week. There is music playing in the background to create a celebratory mood and the session ends with a quick and easy 30-minute game of football.

A first-time participant often leaves with a smile, having ticked off a workout while meeting a bunch of strangers who they can now call friends. “You feel like, ‘Oh, I can actually play football and want to get better. I can’t wait to come back for the next session’,” Hans says. “Honestly, just being at the session opens doors for connection. It happens very naturally, and by the end of 90 minutes, you feel you belong here.”

Beyond nurturing new connections, Sisters in Sweat offers women something increasingly rare in India’s densely populated tier 1 cities: access to third spaces where they can show up and move their bodies without fear of judgment or safety concerns. With India’s fitness market projected to grow from $12.3bn (£9.2bn) in 2024 to $23.2bn by 2030 – an 88.6% increase over six years – Sisters in Sweat’s growth and expansion reflect the broader industry trend.

“My cousin, who is from the UK, was actively involved in our Sisters in Sweat sessions while she was in India on holiday. But after she returned to the UK, she wasn’t able to find a community like that,” Subbiah says. “I have heard the same thing from friends in Singapore and other countries. So, I think we, in many ways, have been the first movers to identify this.”

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

At the heart of Sisters in Sweat’s aim is to fill the gaping hole left by Indian women dropping out of sport, especially after school or college. In the country’s deeply patriarchal social structure, many women are often discouraged from venturing outdoors alone or playing sport recreationally. For many, having the freedom to stay out late at night is a distant dream or a luxury, at best.

“Once a woman leaves her role as a student, she moves on to her next role in life, which is typically becoming a wife,” Subbiah, who has been a Nike coach for over a decade, says. “Then she takes on all the household duties. Add a kid into the mix, and her personal time is minimised.

“There is also immense pressure on a lot of Indian women not to go out or play outdoors because they could catch a tan and look less appealing. A lot of the work we’ve done is to push past these social constructs and say, “Get a tan, it’s beautiful. Come out and play with us, you’ll feel great.”

The TNT Sports presenter and Brighton fan on why the Seagulls should dare to dream

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

This season, I think I’ve lost count of the amount of times someone has come up to me and said, “Brighton are in the title race, aren’t they?” Whether they’ve been joking or not, the fact they’ve included the club in the conversation is bonkers. We’ve enjoyed the adulation – it was deserved after an impressive run of results to start the season.

Brighton have begun the campaign as entertainers. Fabian Hurzeler has them free-scoring, upsetting the Premier League champions and playing an attacking brand of football that’s fun to watch.

Most Albion fans have been realistic that mounting a title challenge is one step too far. What does feel possible though, and it still feels crazy that I’m even writing this, is that there’s probably never been a better opportunity to challenge for a Champions League place – madness for a club that only experienced European football for the first time in its history in 2023.

On top of the Seagulls’ great start, some of the usual contenders for the Champions League places didn’t really get going early on. Manchester United and Spurs both struggled, Liverpool and Chelsea were still settling under new managers, and Manchester City have been at risk of being hit with sanctions this term. If ever there was a season where a disruptor could break into those qualification spots, it’s this one. Brighton will be one of the favourites to do it.

I’ll be honest and admit that before a ball was even kicked, I was nervous about this season. As fans, we’re used to losing key players and coping pretty well, but to lose the spine of Jan Paul van Hecke, Carlos Baleba and Danny Welbeck all in the same window was a big blow. Joao Pedro was sold the summer before, and losing both the Brazilian and Welbeck in successive summers without an experienced replacement felt risky.

Scoring goals was a huge concern, but I’ve been proven completely wrong. Again. The club have shown once more that they’re not just one step ahead of everyone else, but two. They had their best ever start to a top-flight season, and over the first seven league games of the campaign, only Barcelona and Bayern Munich had scored more among Europe’s top five leagues.

Brighton consistently find hidden gems. It’s a testament to their recruitment policy and they appear to have done it again with a number of players. The club don’t mind marketing themselves as one that helps a player progress and allows them to leave if a big offer arises, and their culture provides young talent a platform to thrive without too much pressure.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Greek teenage striker Charalampos Kostoulas looks like one of the best young players in the league and is key to Hurzeler’s aggressive press. Also just 19 years old, no-one expected Luka Vuskovic to replace Van Hecke so well. They are two young players who are flourishing in a team that also has plenty of experience in captain Lewis Dunk and Pascal Gross to give it the right balance.

Brighton’s stand-out performer has been 35-year-old Gross, who returned to the club in a genius January move after a season-and-a-half at Borussia Dortmund. His workrate, and goal and assist output had already given him legendary status at the Amex, but he’s been on another level and is clearly enjoying his football more than ever.

There have already been a handful of memorable results, including the comeback win at Old Trafford, a 3-0 victory at home to Arsenal and a 5-0 thrashing of rivals Crystal Palace, which included that halfway line goal from Diego Gomez. It will go down as one of the all-time great Premier League strikes and summed up the confidence Brighton are playing with.

The challenge now is to compete consistently and stay in this crazy conversation as long as possible. As fans, we always expect a bad run just around the corner, but this season could be special. The club are Conference League favourites, and supporters are desperate to see a first major trophy.

Football is there to make us believe and Brighton fans will continue to dream after the start we’ve seen. There may never be a better opportunity to break into the Champions League than now, but lifting that first piece of silverware surely has to be a priority.

#1015. How will the USMNT replace Mauricio Pochettino? There’s no clear answer

The USMNT head coach is on the verge of sealing a move to Manchester United, but it’s hard to know who could be in the chair next

Even before the 2026 World Cup, the US Soccer Federation projected an air of confidence in its ability to, someday, replace Mauricio Pochettino.

“We have a process of, on a regular basis, always reviewing sort of succession planning for all of our key roles at US Soccer,” JT Batson, the federation CEO, told ESPN in April. “We’re ready when anything happens, whether it’s CFO, whether it’s a head coach or anything in between.”

Now, it’s time to put those words to the test. Pochettino’s exit is now seemingly a formality, with Manchester United having agreed a deal with him to replace Michael Carrick, who was fired on Thursday.

Upon hiring Pochettino, US Soccer was lauded for garnering the interest of such a respected manager. Few coaches in the men’s game are discussed in similar esteem: such status requires a record of success, a history of having built a stable culture and some unquantifiable aura. Throughout his two years with the US, program mainstays spoke glowingly about how Pochettino had changed the culture around the team following Gregg Berhalter’s six years in the role.

In total, Pochettino’s half-cycle term has warped expectations of the ideal profile for a USMNT coach. It’s an expensive evolution, but one that can’t be discounted as the US enter the 2030 World Cup cycle.

Who, exactly, makes sense to sustain the momentum he’s built?

The first name on many fans’ lips. He’s long been at the top of hypothetical wishlists, having spent a year’s sojourn in New York City between leaving Bayern Munich and beginning his decade with Manchester City. There have been rumors for years that he may be interested in leading the US at a home World Cup if his time with City ended beforehand. That timeline didn’t quite come to pass, but he’s unattached now and is the only unemployed manager who would universally be seen as an upgrade over Pochettino.

Then again, the reasons that made Pochettino lasting a full four years in this job seem outlandish are even more relevant to Guardiola, who turned down the Italy job this summer. While Concacaf has improved over the past decade, it’s still among the world’s least esteemed confederations and lacks the hallowed continental championships of Europe, South America, Africa and Asia. Would three and a half years of friendlies, an easier World Cup qualifying path than ever, and routine matchups with Mexico and Canada be enough to whet his competitive appetite until 2030?

Bear in mind, Guardiola – and another available celebrity manager, Antonio Conte – only reach this status by being workaholics. These are obsessives who kneel at the altar of the almighty grind. With respect to the Gold Cup and the Nations League, this just may not be the standard of project that could appease such ambition. Concacaf’s lesser global status could also repel the next tier of proven international managers, which could include Rudi Garcia, Sebastián Beccacece and Diego Alonso.

Historically, the USMNT have avoided questions of devotion by leaning into the domestic coaching pool. When Bruce Arena first took the role in 1998, he had just started MLS’s first dynasty. By the time Bob Bradley took over in 2006, he was also among the league’s winningest coaches. When Gregg Berhalter was hired after the failure to qualify for Russia 2018, he was a universally rated option whose race was run in Columbus.

The most qualified American for the job, by nearly every criteria, has almost certainly disqualified himself from contention. Rare is the international window where Canada head coach Jesse Marsch isn’t asked for his thoughts on the USMNT, or US politics, or what beating Canada’s southern rivals means to him on a personal level. Even scarcer is the instance where his answer doesn’t spur a myriad of headlines.

“Let me make it really clear: I never will coach the US national team. Ever,” Jesse Marsch, Canada head coach, told Time magazine in July. “And that’s no problem. There was the possibility of me at one point, but I’m done with it. I don’t even care any more.”

If Marsch has a rival for “best active American men’s coach”, it’s Pellegrino Matarazzo. The New Jersey native graduated from Columbia University and promptly began a playing career in Germany, where he also launched his coaching career. After successful stops at Stuttgart and Hoffenheim, Matarazzo is at the helm of Real Sociedad, where he became the first US manager to win a trophy in Europe’s big five leagues by lifting the Copa Del Rey last spring. If the US came calling, Sociedad would probably work to keep him.

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

In between Berhalter’s first and second terms, BJ Callaghan led the US to win the Gold Cup with eye-catching play and impressive control over games. He took his first club head coaching job in 2024, and has since turned Nashville SC into a record-setting team favored to win a rare domestic double this postseason.

Nashville signed Callaghan to a fresh extension in February, locking him into terms through the 2028-29 MLS season. His possession-heavy style of play remains en vogue in the international game. But at this stage, the 45-year-old may revel in his current project for a bit longer.

After Callaghan, the options almost entirely skew towards MLS coaches and few have CVs that could retain players’ enthusiasm after Pochettino’s exit. Steve Cherundolo, a former US defender and the current U-20/U-23 boss, won an MLS Cup, but his Los Angeles FC tenure was more largely characterized by tactical timidness and failing to dictate proceedings in the biggest games.

Even broadening the scope to coaches with MLS success in spite of their passport does little to unearth obvious fits. Wilfried Nancy has arguably been MLS’s best coach this decade, but his intricate style of play would struggle to translate given the stop/start nature of international soccer. The same could be said for the Vancouver Whitecaps’ Jesper Sørensen.

Thierry Henry may be an intriguing candidate. Henry struggled in club coaching roles with Monaco and Montreal, but reveled in the task of leading France’s U-23s to a silver medal at a home Olympics. The relatively occasional nature of international windows may not be a hindrance, and he’s expressed admiration for MLS and the US national team in the past. Antonio Conte has had no connection whatsoever with the US program, but could be a potential option should the federation have donor money to put towards a top-class coaching hire, as they did with Pochettino.

Regardless of which way they go, the path forward is far from clear.

#1013. Ian Holloway’s circus: why the manager’s antics are no laughing matter for fans

Swindon manager has a history of viral outbursts but fans want a united club and manager they can support

In Ian Holloway’s often madcap managerial orbit, this was simply the latest in a steady succession of eccentric outbursts. Eyes bulging as he spoke, he boomed the letter “D” and promptly stabbed himself in the chest with an imaginary dagger. Next came the letter “M” alongside a blow from another invisible knife. Finally, a “W” followed by a jab to the heart. “Dead. Man. Walking,” he declared, pausing for effect between words and briefly falling into an Oscar-worthy zombie stupor. “That’s how it feels.”

To an offbeat press conference genre containing seagulls following trawlers and self-proclaimed special ones, it was a crazy new entry worthy of its subsequent viral nature. Holloway at his finest.

The clip was widely shared, there is every chance you saw it this month. The general perception, from those of a neutral stance, was that one of football’s great characters had lost the plot. To those in the room, there was a sense that it was merely the exuberant mannerisms of a quirky manager during a tricky period. But for a large section of Swindon fans, it prompted an unamused eye roll. Here we go again. The circus tent is pitched firmly in town.

Supporting a Holloway-led club is an interesting assignment. Within weeks of taking the Swindon job two years ago on Sunday, he began constructing a hostile wall towards fans by reminding them that they could “go bowling” if they did not like his methods. Last December, he had to be restrained by his players during an altercation with a fan, while he has made a habit of telling them to “jog on” if overly vocal in their criticism.

When his side picked up a much-needed point against Walsall last week, the goalkeeping coach held him back from another confrontation with supporters. Asked about it, he goaded reporters into putting his address online so that disgruntled fans could have it out with him: “I don’t really care anymore.” So, when season‑ticket holders found their phones pinging with amused messages containing the same viral Holloway zombie clip, their lack of laughter could be forgiven.

“When you get these soundbites from Ian Holloway, outside the Swindon Town world it’s all about what a great character he is, how he says it like it is, and how it must be great to have him as manager,” says Rich Pullen, founder and co-host of the largest Swindon podcast, Loathed Strangers. “But, to a growing percentage of the Swindon community, it’s exhausting and it takes away from any of the good.

“If Swindon win, post-match he often uses it as an opportunity to have a go at the fans. It’s got to the stage where you can’t even enjoy a win without Ian Holloway being unable to hold himself from criticising fans. The easy thing to do is ignore him, but it’s almost impossible because he is everywhere. He goes viral and everyone always thinks: ‘Oh, isn’t that funny.’ Well, no. People are tired of the excess noise.”

This time last week, there was a thought that the M4 derby homecoming trip to Bristol Rovers on Saturday might hasten a possible end to Holloway’s Swindon tenure. Winless in eight games in all competitions, the discontent was not expected to abate on the preceding midweek trip to high-flying Barnet. The 3-1 victory that followed – Barnet’s first league defeat of the season – was a huge shock, thanks in no small part to the heroics of the goalkeeper, Connor Ripley, who recently declared the whole squad would “run through a brick wall” for Holloway.

Swindon might have followed it with another win, at Rovers’ Memorial Stadium, only for Matty Virtue to miss an open goal 90 seconds into the match. The forgettable goalless draw that played out at least extended Swindon’s unbeaten run to three games and kept them safely mid-table in League Two. Holloway was right to savour the improved performances, but the malaise runs deeper.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

The manager had said something far more significant immediately after his viral soundbite when he continued: “The owner’s a dead man walking as well and that over‑complicates everything here.”

Even those seeking a more composed figure in Holloway’s place agree the manager is just one cog in a machine many argue has been misfiring for some time. Days after the zombie rant, the Swindon Town Supporters Trust declared the club had “lost our soul, our hope, our passion”, and urged Holloway’s comments about the Australian owner, Clem Morfuni, to “be a wake-up call”.

Since saving the club from probable administration in 2021, Morfuni has become a target of increasing fan indignation, failing to sell up and adding millions to the club’s debt. “Whilst the short-term focus may be on Ian Holloway, the bigger picture is above the role of the manager,” concluded the Trust, pointing to “a wedge with supporters so obvious that even the manager openly talks about it”.

In such a context, the uptick in form is merely one – albeit very welcome – aspect among wider misgivings. Because what fans really want is a united club and manager they can get behind; not to go jogging on.

#1012. Mauricio Pochettino reveals when Man United contacted him about replacing Michael Carrick

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Pochettino was confirmed as Michael Carrick’s successor at Man United on Friday

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Mauricio Pochettino struggled to fight off tears as he held his first press conference since being confirmed as Michael Carrick’s managerial successor at Manchester United.

Pochettino will leave his post as United States manager at the end of the current international break, joining up with United on 18 November following the club’s move to replace Carrick, who was sacked on Thursday.

Pochettino penned a four-year extension in the summer that was meant to keep him with the USA until the 2030 World Cup, but United triggered his release clause after hashing out an agreement with the Argentinian, and will pay US Soccer compensation worth an initial $7m (£5.3m).

Asked what made him swap the USA for United despite committing his future earlier this year, Pochettino said: “It’s obvious. I never said I wanted to go back but they know there aren’t too many opportunities that happen in your career like Manchester United. When it arrives, it’s difficult to turn down.

“When we decided together to extend our commitment, it was a commitment for the federation, just in case. We were very committed. It was to help the federation, just in case that didn’ work for four years."

Pochettino said contact from United was first made on Sunday afternoon, the same day as the Villa draw, insisting that he was “very transparent” with US Soccer throughout the process.

“All was so quick. Sunday afternoon, there started to be some contact. We were very transparent [with US Soccer],” he said. “We’ll have time next week to talk about the job at Manchester United. It’s much better to talk now about US Soccer.”

The former Tottenham and Chelsea manager opted against speaking at length about his United move, which he described as “the most difficult decisions of my career”, instead focusing on Haiti and his time in the USA setup. “We have two games ahead and now it’s focus on this."

Pochettino will remain in charge for the United States’ two Concacaf Nations League fixtures against Haiti during the international break, with an away match on 14 November and a home match in Cincinnati on 18 November. He will then report to Carrington shortly after, with his official start date being 18 November, ahead of United’s next Premier League match against Liverpool at Anfield on 22 November.

He also explained why he decided to see out the rest of the international break in the USA dugout, saying it was out of respect for his players and staff.

“Because before [we are] professional, we are a person,” he added. “The emotional link between us is to show the commitment and respect and the love, even if we take a decision that is not the best for one part.

“We have the respect of the players and the staff and they understand the situation. It’s Manchester United and the federation agrees on different terms. All of the games are important. We are brave enough to go ahead because we are optimistic and very positive. We need to play tomorrow and the next game. We need to perform.”

#1011. Mourinho’s plan comes together as Real Madrid relaunch with clásico statement | Sid Lowe

It was just like old times as José Mourinho ended a night at Camp Nou with a knee slide and three points

José Mourinho had already done the por qué?, the printout and the press conference no-show in under 100 days. Now he’s done a knee slide too, and in the perfect place: back where it all began and where it can all begin again. When Kylian Mbappé scored the first in the clásico on Sunday night, Real Madrid’s manager hardly moved, sitting in the shadow of the bench – but when the striker got the second to win it with time running out, that was different. Mourinho leapt into the light, throwing himself to the grass, the knees of a 63-year-old’s trousers muddy as a schoolboy’s, stuck his tongue out and pumped his fists.

He does so love it when a plan comes together. To the right of him, the bench was emptying, subs joining the players in sprinting towards the south-west corner. As they leapt about, dodging the bottles thrown towards them from the end, way, way up in the furthest corner and stuck inside a glass box like a bunch of David Blaines, the small group of Madrid fans who had come were going mad. In the main stand, a thousand phones were raised. And 600 kilometres west, back in Boadilla, Thibaut Courtois was watching his teammates from the sofa at home, presumably wrapped in a blanket and cradling a cup of Lemsip. On the morning of the biggest game there is, he awoke with flu, forced to miss out.

“We have the best goalkeeper in the world, but none of us cried because Thibaut couldn’t play,” Mourinho said. Plenty might have felt like it, more reason to be fearful. But the coach called Andriy Lunin, the substitute goalkeeper so serious that he bought a roll of artificial turf and spent the pandemic diving round the living room of his flat, and told him this was his moment: “You train to play, not to sit on the bench, so go on.” As for the rest of them, the manager told them nothing changes: the plan remains in place. By the time they headed back to the dressing room, “Fucking get in!” echoing along the Camp Nou corridor, so it had proved.

Thirteen years later, Mourinho was back in Barcelona for a clásico and he had guided Madrid to a 2-1 win. It wasn’t supposed to be like this, or maybe it was. Barcelona, the team who had won nine in a row, banging in 4.3 goals per game, had been beaten by Madrid, the team who had lost twice already and, truth be told, were mostly just not very good. The night it could have been all over, the title race done when it’s not even in November, was instead the night it finally started. “If you leave here nine points behind, it’s very heavy psychologically; if it’s six, it’s more balanced; if it’s three, that’s different,” Mourinho said.

This was different, and so is the season now. Counting the clásicos all those years ago, Mourinho racked up his sixth consecutive meeting with Barcelona without defeat, and there had been no parked bus, nor many lumps kicked. They didn’t just desperately hang on, although there was a moment when Dean Huijsen saved a shot with his face. Nor had they just waited for a moment, resisting and then robbing it, even if João Cancelo did insist: “That’s Madrid; they don’t have many chances but they score them.” The final shot count said 18-10 to Barcelona, and possession was 62% Barcelona’s.

“The way we won is important: you can win luckily or by defending a lot. But we won with calmness and totally deservedly. We did it by being organised, concentrated and having the courage to come out from the back,” Mourinho said. And if that might have been pushing it a little – and, let’s face it, the analyses might be different had Lunin not made an astonishing save from Gerard Martín or Lamine Yamal’s second-half shot not faded just past the post – he had a point.

Barcelona were not at their best. They had been hurried and imprecise, Rodri telling his teammates to lower their “pulse rate” as they came out for the second half. Lamine Yamal somehow missed an extraordinary chance just before the break. And when they did tighten the screw in the second half, they couldn’t break the wall. Xavi Espart was forced off, yet another injury at the back, the failure to sign a centre-back in the spotlight again. Yet this was still a faster, more aggressive, tighter Madrid than anyone expected. Asked to define it, Lunin went for “discipline and attitude”. And if that is partly about occasion, the least you can ask for, it’s more than you sometimes get.

Besides, it was also more than that. More than Marc Cucurella getting under Lamine Yamal’s skin, although he certainly succeeded. They went for the space beyond Barcelona’s full-backs: superb in his first clásico, aged 19, Yan Diomandé – the left winger – got more touches than any Madrid player, and protected his full-back as well. But it was more than that, too. More than the wonderful winning goal, a flash of inspiration with Jude Bellingham going all Nureyev, the ball flitting between his feet and Gabriel Jesus’s legs, pirouetting to release Eduardo Camavinga. This was a team with an idea and a victory that vindicated their manager, some kind of resurrection.

Before the game, Rodri said that one of Madrid’s tricks is to convince you that they’re not that good, but insisted he wouldn’t fall into that trap. Still he felt that plan particularly. Pedri did too. Bellingham dealt with Rodri, Bernardo Silva with Pedri. Pressed and tired too, according to Hansi Flick, neither truly took control. The inclusion of Arda Güler and Silva – the surprise in the middle, starting his first league game in six weeks – underlined an intention for Madrid to keep the ball when they could. They actually had a midfield, which was new. From the back they tried to build, draw Barcelona in. And if a time came when they had to wait, to put bodies in before the ball, well, they would do that too. Six times Barcelona shots were blocked. At least twice more, shots were taken from their toes. At the other end, meanwhile, Madrid attacked with an intent and an incision that probably drew the clearer chances: the xG showed 1.19 v 1.94.

Alaves 1-1 Malaga, Rayo Vallecano 0-3 Elche, Racing Santander 2-1 Espanyol, Valencia 1-2 Villarreal, Atlético 1-0 Deportiva A Coruna, A Bilbao 4-0 Getafe, Celta Vigo 0-0 Real Betis, Real Sociedad 2-1 Levante, Barcelona 1-2 Real Madrid

Victory puts Madrid three points behind Barcelona and, Federico Valverde claimed, “will give us a kickstart”. It has taken 10 weeks but it’s game on. Hay liga, as they like to say. There is league. There is Madrid, too. Something has shifted, starting in Rome, where 70 dreadful minutes gave way to 20 pretty good ones, another inexplicable comeback actually having something of an explanation, too. The changes were impossible to ignore. Valverde and Aurélien Tchouaméni no longer the partnership in the middle, Valverde going to right-back instead. Güler playing. Diomandé playing. And, yes, Vinícius Júnior not playing. “I’m not stubborn; I can change,” Mourinho said. Madrid have won five in succession now; something was seen that night, a way ahead. They’ve won every game since Vinícius was suspended, facile and perhaps even cruel though that may be to say. And since Mourinho grew a beard, if you believe in that kind of thing.

Before the clásico, Mourinho had said it wasn’t fair to compare his team, a side in construction and a long way from the finished product, to Barcelona. He insisted that he was still getting to know his players; he hadn’t been there long, after all. After the clásico, he admitted: “We have improved, we can’t hide that.” The idea has shifted, almost like it was an epiphany: “I’ve learned something about the middle of the pitch; I have learned that a mixture is better, that it is better to have a combination of qualities than two players of similar characteristics.” In short, Tchouaméni and Valverde doesn’t work. There needs to be some football in there somewhere, and so a shift started. Sunday came as a kind of confirmation, a hope, an identity emerging.

“The best Madrid is born at the Camp Nou,” ran the headline in El País. “Madrid are here now,” AS’s cover said. “I won’t let them have their heads on the moon; if we win this and then don’t win at the Sardinero, it won’t mean much,” Mourinho said, but this was a start, not just an end in itself. At full time, Mourinho headed on to the pitch and shook Lunin’s hand as all around players embraced. High in the north-east corner, Madrid’s fans stayed and sang. Back home, Courtois was watching. He had “a horrible night” on Saturday, they said, but now he was feeling a little better. They all were.

Newcastle United sit in mid-table after 10 games this season but the picture could be a whole lot bleaker by the New Year

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Sitting bottom of the Premier League’s Expected Points (xPTS) table is cause for concern at St James' Park this season.

Newcastle United’s high-risk tactical approach under new head coach Matthias Jaissle has left them exposed in transition, but their biggest structural weakness appears when they are forced onto the back foot. The team has largely relied on a single way of playing so far, with little in the way of an effective direct outlet when opponents pin them deep.

The root of the issue is highlighted in data published by Twitter/X user @markrstats who has examined how Premier League forwards perform when contesting long balls. The data visualisation plots volume (how often a forward is first to a long clearance per 90 minutes) against security (how often the forward's team retains possession).

Across the division, Newcastle’s attacking options register some of the weakest numbers in the league.

Matias Fernandez-Pardo ranks lowest in the below dataset for ball retention. While he contests an average of 2.8 long balls per 90 minutes, Newcastle retain possession following his involvement just 27% of the time. In practical terms, roughly three out of every four long balls targeted toward Fernandez-Pardo result in a turnover of possession.

Brian Brobbey is the best target man in the Premier League this season When Sunderland go long from their own half and he gets to the ball first, they keep it 79% of the time. The average for forwards is 53%. Calvert-Lewin, who wins far more long balls, is at 53%, Delap at 38% https://t.co/Q5Ftm51HOxNovember 8, 2026

Yoane Wissa offers even less presence in these situations. The DR Congo forward is first to just 1.2 long balls per 90 minutes - the lowest of any forward evaluated in the graphic.

His retention rate of roughly 41.5% is an improvement on Fernandez-Pardo, but his low involvement means Newcastle rarely look in his direction when clearing the ball from deep.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

By comparison, effective direct outlets offer either high-volume contesting or a high level of security. Dominic Calvert-Lewin contests 7.1 long balls per 90 for Leeds United, with a 53% retention rate, while Sunderland’s Brian Brobbey combines 4.9 long balls per 90 with a league-leading 79% retention rate.

Newcastle possess neither attribute in their current starting frontline.

This lack of aerial presence can leave the side trapped in their own half whenever an opposing press successfully cuts off short passing options - which is not a place any team wants to find themselves. Without a forward who can pin a centre-back or win an initial duel, Newcastle cannot move up the pitch as a unit.

Newcastle's squad does, however, contain a profile capable of addressing this shortcoming in Will Osula.

Standing at well over 6ft tall, the Danish international offers the physical profile Newcastle are currently missing centrally.

In his Premier League minutes, Osula has averaged 4.35 successful aerial duels per 90 - the highest among all Newcastle players, ahead of central defenders Dan Burn (4.00) and Sven Botman.

His aerial duel success rate regularly exceeds 70%, offering the target man traits required to bring supporting runners into play.

When he has started this season, Newcastle have looked more of a threat, including in the season opener at home to Liverpool, and the 2-0 away win against Crystal Palace.

Playing exclusively through transition and pressing is not yet generating reliable results for the Magpies. Unless Newcastle change their attacking style and deploy more of a reference point like Osula to make long balls stick, their lack of a direct alternative could drag them into a relegation fight.

#1007. Rampant Salford hint that Beckham’s lofty ambitions are not a pipe dream

The aim of reaching the Championship looks more realistic for a Manchester club in the shadow of City and United

After seven seasons in League Two, Salford City are finally threatening to match the hype brought by their high-profile owners. First it was the Class of ’92 who guided them up through the non-league system into the fourth tier but failed to progress any further. Gary Neville and David Beckham remain, part of a new group that took over in May 2025, with this year beginning to look transformational after securing an eighth straight win, against Exeter, to put them five points clear at the top.

The budget has increased, allowing the club to sign a number of players who will feel they are above League Two standard. Striker Macaulay Langstaff arrived from Millwall; the last time he played at this level, he scored 28 league goals in a season for Notts County. Match-winner Will Aimson spent the past two seasons in the division above with Wigan and has dropped down because of Salford’s project.

In terms of personnel, the most notable change was in the dugout where 48-year-old Peter Cklamovski replaced Karl Robinson, who was sacked after a desperate performance in the playoff final loss to Notts County. Cklamovski’s previous experience came working under Ange Postecoglou before becoming a head coach in his own right in Asia, most recently taking charge of the Malaysia national team. Such was his unknown status, Salford’s chief football adviser Paul Scholes had to Google the Australian before he was appointed.

Off the pitch, Salford reverted to wearing orange, the traditional club colour that was changed by the Class of ’92, who wanted the shirts to reflect their links to Manchester United. The fans voted for it, democracy in action where previously the owners knew best. Beckham has turned Inter Miami into a global brand worth more than £1bn, making pink a key part of its identity. Lionel Messi shirt sales helped the hue travel, with kids across the UK spotted with the famous No 10 on the back. Beckham selected the shade of orange – and the badge was redesigned – but whether Langstaff et al can have the same effect as Messi remains to be seen. “Not many others play in orange, so if you’re going to see that kit around Manchester, you would know it’s not United or City,” says Danny Shepherd of The Future Is Orange podcast.

Attracting new fans is the aim but Salford face competition from much bigger clubs in the region. Even with Manchester City in a crisis and United’s form spiralling, convincing locals to head down to the AIG Stadium is difficult. Cklamovski’s attractive style is a deliberate ploy but the Ammies have the fourth-worst average attendance in League Two. It is optimistic to think they can create a Championship fanbase, even with subsidised away travel.

Cklamovski is making a name for himself with the aggressive attacking football he learned under his mentor. He started with three defeats but since then the Australian has found a pragmatic approach, mixing his playing out from the back ideals with an openness to be more direct when required, which brought a change in fortunes.

“I’d be disappointed if we didn’t go up because of the strength in depth,” says Shepherd. “Last season we had certain linchpin players that if they weren’t available, then we had either a utility player, a youngster or someone whose quality is so much lower that it’s like falling off a cliff. I’m not a rose-tinted spectacles fan, I can’t see how this team cannot get promoted – I think we should win the league at a canter.”

The confidence was not fully apparent in the first half as Salford were sloppy and struggled to create chances, while defensively vulnerable against a resolute Exeter. Goalkeeper Will Norris was booked for rushing out of his area and fouling Sonny Cox, who got his own back by scoring the opener for a side on a fine run themselves, unbeaten in the previous five.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Salford only came to life after the disappointing Luke Molyneux was forced off through injury, replaced by Daniel Udoh in the 55th minute. Energy levels increased and were rewarded by Luke Garbutt’s leveller at the back post after Langstaff’s fine work on the right.

Salford were on top after that and got their reward from the unfamiliar source of former Exeter centre-back Aimson, who sent a shot into the top corner from 25 yards to keep the run going and show this team have character to battle back in difficult circumstances. “We’ve got to stay really focused and diligent,” Cklamovski says. “We’ve got a nice bit of momentum, but don’t look too far forward. Eight wins in a row or 11 unbeaten however you want to look at it, just don’t look back.” He need not worry, there are plenty of people above him looking to the future.

#1003. Man Utd confirm Mauricio Pochettino start date after deal agreed to succeed Michael Carrick

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Pochettino takes the reins at Old Trafford as he departs his role as United States national team manager

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Manchester United have appointed Mauricio Pochettino as their new manager.

The club confirmed their decision to sack Michael Carrick after just 10 games of the season on Thursday, with the club dwindling in 18th heading into the international break.

United have paid US Soccer compensation worth an initial $7m (£5.3m) to get Pochettino out of his existing contract, which ran until the 2030 World Cup. Additional compensation will be required for Pochettino’s trusted coaching staff, including long-time assistant Jesus Perez.

"The opportunity to represent the USA crest was one of the greatest honors of my career,” Pochettino said after his departure and move to Man United was confirmed.

“We are so grateful to the players for their commitment, to the fans for their belief, and to the Federation for always supporting our staff and creating the opportunities to impact the culture of soccer in this great country,” Pochettino said. “We want to thank Cindy Parlow Cone, JT Batson and Dan Helfrich for their partnership and incredible working relationships throughout our time here.

“There is tremendous talent in the U.S. player pool from the youth teams through to the senior team, and it’s one of the reasons we have so much belief for the future of U.S. Soccer. You will always have a special place in our hearts, and we will be supporting the teams whenever they step on the field."

He will remain in charge for the United States’ two Concacaf Nations League fixtures against Haiti during the international break, with an away match on 14 November and a home match in Cincinnati on 18 November.

Pochettino will then report to Carrington shortly after, with his official start date being on 18 November, ahead their next Premier League match against Liverpool at Anfield on 22 November.

While losing Pochettino is blow for the USA, The Independent understands that US Soccer has been prepared for the prospect of his exit at some stage before the 2030 World Cup, with a succession plan already in place.

Pochettino arrives at Old Trafford with the club in crisis yet again, having won just once in the Premier League this season, against Ipswich Town, and gained only eight points from the first 10 matches.

Carrick still held goodwill with the fanbase before his sacking despite the dire run of form, with frustration targeted at the ownership and the board. United bosses nevertheless called time on his reign after the latest round of crisis talks in Monaco this week.

Pochettino last managed in the English top-flight during the 2023/24 season, when he guided Chelsea to a sixth-place finish despite spending a lot of the campaign struggling in mid-table. He left by mutual consent at the end of the season.

Between his five-year spell at Tottenham - where he led Spurs to the Champions League final in 2019 - and his single term at Stamford Bridge, Pochettino spent 18 months at Paris Saint-Germain, winning the Ligue 1 title in 2021/22.

He delivered a run to the last-16 for the USA at this summer’s home World Cup, though his side did not escape controversy after striker Folarin Balogun’s red card was controversially overturned following a call from Donald Trump to Fifa president Gianni Infantino.

#1002. Rise of the ‘schooligans’: how a wave of antisocial behaviour threatens non-league football

Teenage ultras are increasingly causing disorder and communities fear it will not be long before it becomes something more dangerous

It is five past three on Saturday afternoon and the teenage ultras of Hednesford Town are running late. They have arrived in Chester for their team’s National League North fixture and have hailed taxis, determined to make their presence felt at the ground. But word appears to have got out about their arrival. As one car turns away from the city’s charming half-timbered houses and into narrow residential streets, half a dozen local youths appear, haring round the corner in balaclavas. They try to attack the cab and chase after it as it pulls away. The smell of pyro is everywhere. As the taxi finally gets clear, the Chester gang stops in the middle of the road, shouting and gesticulating. One lad, no older than 16, pulls a long blade from inside his trousers and brandishes it.

The incident ended there and no one was hurt, though a police investigation has been launched. The match went off without trouble too and the Hednesford gang – known at home as the “schooligans” – were escorted safely back to the station by Cheshire police. It was just another weekend in English non-league football, where a wave of antisocial behaviour is causing concern and leading the UK Football Policing Unit (UKFPU) to declare it its “most important” priority. As the disorder continues, a question remains: how long will it be before teenage trouble-making becomes something more dangerous?

This year clubs from the south coast to the north-east have reported disorder caused by supporters under the age of 18, some seemingly as young as 10. In February, Aldershot Town experienced a series of disorderly incidents involving young people that included brawls outside the ground, behaviour the club described as “wholly unacceptable and [which] will not be tolerated”. In August, Enfield Town said they were “concerned and disappointed” by young fans at a fixture in Lewes. Two weeks ago, a Gloucester City fan was hit by a rock thrown by teenagers at Redditch United during an FA Trophy tie. Even Soham Town Rangers of the ninth-tier Eastern Counties League urged parents to ensure their children make “sensible choices” ahead of a match against Mildenhall Town.

Hednesford have experienced consistent trouble for a number of seasons and in August their owner and chair, Craig Gwilt, attempted to face it down. A rising tide of disorder was harming the club, he said, behaviour that included “pitch invasions, fighting, abuse directed towards players, missiles being thrown at opposition goalkeepers, flares entering the field of play and even interference with players’ water bottles”. He called on fans to improve their behaviour or risk permanently damaging the club. The plea was not immediately heard. Three weeks after Gwilt’s statement the club banned 20 young supporters from attending matches after there was action away at Telford.

Hednesford is a town of 19,000 people on the edge of the protected landscape of Cannock Chase. The town centre is neat and tidy, a well-maintained monument to the Stafford regiment at its heart. On the way to the ground you can get a pint at the Cross Keys where Dick Turpin reputedly rested his head. It’s a town seemingly at peace with itself and the club is at the heart of the community. But both are struggling to get to grips with an issue that leaves people scratching their heads.

This season the club have introduced measures to prevent under-16s from entering without an accompanying adult. There is also extra security on matchdays, ostensibly to manage car parking. These interventions appear to have contained any trouble in and around the stadium, but now gangs of up to 50 youths will gather post-match at a safe remove to look for trouble or, more likely, save their energy for an away fixture. Like the one at Chester, for example, when the schooligans were removed from one train for antisocial behaviour and were drinking alcohol throughout their journey up. Encountering such groups on a Saturday will be familiar to many rail passengers.

The schooligans, whose nickname was coined by Hednesford’s security staff, “baffle” the club’s chief executive, Marvin Robinson, who would rather be spending his time modernising a club that have had back-to-back promotions. “I’m not really sure I understand why it seems to be a trend,” he says. “It’s a wider social issue but what is it and what will it become? Is it a social media thing? Is it about notoriety or becoming known for something? The adult response online has been almost to normalise it. I don’t agree with that.”

Go on TikTok and the picture does start to become a little clearer. From aggregator accounts to individual semi-anonymised accounts belonging to the teenagers, there is a wealth of posts celebrating the behaviour of “top lads” who “mooch” to the ground before “running” the opposition out of town. Often set to a backing of euphoric electronic dance music with a layer or two of visual effects and captions such as “this weekend’s got me feeling like a little kid at Christmas”, the posts are celebratory and almost nostalgic in tone. In recent weeks TikTok has begun appending disclaimers to them that read: “Participating in this activity could result in you or others getting hurt.” TikTok removed an account named “NLN [National League North] gimps and chants”, when alerted to it by the Guardian, for contravening guidelines that do not allow content that glorifies violence.

The mythology of old-school football hooliganism appears to be well‑known among these groups, with references to the 2005 film Green Street commonplace. But the schooligans of 2026 don’t behave like the firms of the past. For a start they rarely, if at all, arrange to fight their rivals. Instead they use the mapping feature on Snapchat to alert opposition to their presence on the day, and take it from there. The concept of rivalry itself is fluid. In the West Midlands, for example, teens from Hednesford will band together with those nominally affiliated with Redditch or Cannock Town. When there was trouble recently at Hednesford’s fixture at Hereford, local police said the majority of disorder had been caused by Redditch fans chasing supporters from Solihull Moors. It isn’t just local either. Children as young as 12 have been detained in the north-west having travelled from the south coast, a distance of more than 200 miles.

The chair of Redditch, David Faulkner, is still dealing with the fallout from the Gloucester tie two weeks ago. He says the fluid set of alliances between ultra groups has created a “travelling circus” and that no one knows where it will turn up next. Branding himself “the non-League chair”, Faulkner has started posting videos on YouTube drawing attention to the disorder and calling for collective action.

“People think of non-league football as one man and his dog, but we need to catch up with the fact that it’s massive now,” Faulkner says. “Some clubs have attendances bigger than in League One but the regulations were put in place decades ago. We need that extra regulation, that support, so we can get the funding to put things like CCTV and more stewarding in place. Because the other way this could go is that [change only happens] when someone gets seriously hurt. I haven’t got metal detectors on our gates to stop kids bringing knives in. None of that stuff. I’d rather take action before something happens.”

The Football Association says the behaviour of fans is primarily a matter for clubs and relevant authorities but that it is working to develop policies that welcome young fans safely to National League grounds. The UK Football Policing Unit, meanwhile, is working alongside leagues and the Crown Prosecution Service to develop new policies around “youth risk”, which are likely to include an extra focus on education via schools and community work.

“It’s probably the most important area of football policing that we’re focused on,” says Mike Ankers, the deputy director of the UKFPU. “We are seeing children as young as 12 or 13 engaged in antisocial behaviour at best, but also actual violence and that’s up and down the country, with some travelling hundreds of miles. There comes a great risk and a great safeguarding issue with regards to that. In terms of our focus, we are making sure that we bring the right people together to have a solution. It’s not just the policing, it requires a more holistic view.”

Ankers says he supports Faulkner in speaking up on the topic and believes many more adults need to take responsibility. “These children need a strong adult role model,” he says. “I would very much question that if your 12-year-old is going out to follow football and is being detained, perhaps 200 miles away, then you need to look at how they’ve been able to travel and have those conversations. I think there’s very much a role for parental responsibility.”

The Hednesford schooligans, having been deposited on the platform at Chester by police, made their way home by train, only to find themselves stuck in a combination of Halloween revellers and national signal failure. Constrained, they hunched over their phones viewing footage from different teenage firms and discussed the day’s events. In the end, they concurred they had got the best of it. After all, said one: “What experience do you get from chasing a taxi?”

TikTok and Snapchat were approached for comment.

#1000. Andy Robertson ties Kenny Dalglish’s Scotland record with 102nd international cap

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Robertson starts against North Macedonia to draw level with Dalglish

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Andy Robertson has drawn level with Sir Kenny Dalglish as Scotland’s most capped player thanks to his appearance against North Macedonia in the Nations League on Friday.

Robertson’s inclusion in the starting XI took him to a 102nd cap and level with Dalglish as the record holder for Scottish players.

Dalglish held the record for 40 years but Robertson can pull ahead on his own if he features against Switzerland in Monday.

The 32-year-old Scotland captain led the team out at Hampden Park to a rapturous reception from the home supporters as he cements his legacy as one of Scotland’s all time great players.

But, Robertson was keen to shine the spotlight away from himself despite the record-equalling occasion in Edinburgh.

"There are normal seats but there's one throne and Kenny Dalglish should be sat on it," Robertson said in the build up to tonight’s match.

"Friday night's not about me. Friday night's about the greatest player of all time in our country, and for me, that will always be Kenny. He's had this record for so long. He deserves it. If he played in a different era, he would probably have played a number of games that wouldn't have been able to be caught.

"Sometimes - not as a criticism - as a country we're maybe not good at recognising how good people we've got are. For me, he's the best player to ever play with Scotland and arguably Britain.

"We have to appreciate that man because I certainly do, my family certainly do and, I think on Friday, I'll have him at the front of my mind, the back of my mind and I'm not really bothered about myself."

Robertson made his debut for Scotland in March 2014 against Poland were he came off the bench as a 19-year-old to replace Barry Bannan in the 67th minute. Scotland won the match 1-0.

He scored his first international goal in his fourth appearance after a flying, and now characteristic, run down the left wing in a losing cause against England but the signs were there that Scotland had birthed another impressive son.

He has awarded the captaincy in 2018 and under manager Steve Clarke led the national team to three major tournaments in five years, culminating in a place at the 2026 World Cup this summer.

With the North Macedonia game his 80th as captain, Robertson is easily Scotland’s most prolific skipper – George Young was the previous record-holder with 48 caps with the armband.

Three Lions great explains why a Tottenham comeback is unlikely for Kane, despite intriguing clause in his new three-year contract

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Harry Kane last night became England’s record appearance-maker – days after signing a new Bayern Munich contract that’s reported to contain an intriguing clause.

Kane followed up his recent Ballon d’Or triumph by winning his 126th cap for his country against Croatia, surpassing Peter Shilton’s long-standing record, and last week he put pen to paper on a new deal keeping him in Germany until 2029.

That will take the striker up to the summer of his 36th birthday, although a key detail of the contract has given Spurs fans a glimmer of hope that he could still return to his former club before the end of his career.

As with his previous deal, it’s been reported that his new contract contains a clause that allows Spurs to match a bid from any other club for his services, should Kane leave Bayern before the summer of 2029.

Former Spurs and England star Chris Waddle doesn’t expect him to return to North London before the end of his career, though.

“People ask me ‘Do you think Harry Kane will go back when he’s 36?’, but why should he go back?” Waddle said.

“He might have a soft spot to go back, but do Tottenham want somebody back at 36 or 37? I don’t think so, even if it is Harry Kane. I think Tottenham are looking to move on and are looking at much younger profiles.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“The Bundesliga is slower than the Premier League, so at 36, he could still be wearing the Bayern Munich No.9 shirt.”

Waddle left Spurs himself to move abroad in 1989, enjoying a successful spell in France with Marseille, and sees how Kane has similarly benefited from playing in a new country.

“He made the right decision, and he probably never thought it would go as well as it has,” said the former winger, speaking in association with iGaming.com.

“When I went to Marseille, I didn’t know what was going to happen, and it turned out to be three unbelievable years in my career.

“I didn’t want to leave Tottenham, but when I look back, it was probably the best move I made. Harry Kane, for all his time with Tottenham – and he loves Tottenham, rightly so – would say that Bayern Munich made him a far better player.”

#996. Next Generation 2021: why slow and steady sometimes wins the race

Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success

Read the full updates on our class of 2021 here and here

In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series.

We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well).

Five years ago we had an exciting array of young players on the list, most of them 17 years old but some 16, with one youngster from Brighton being profiled like this:

double quotation markThe ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players.

It was quite an understated entry, especially compared with this one in the world section:

double quotation markThe youngest to play in the Bundesliga at 16 years and one day, youngest player to appear in the Champions League 17 days later, youngest goal scorer in Bundesliga 11 days after that and youngest player and youngest goal scorer for the Germany Under-21 team before he has turned 17.

Borussia Dortmund’s Youssoufa Moukoko went on to play for Germany at the World Cup the following year, at the same time as Jack Hinshelwood was promoted to the Brighton Under-21s. Different trajectories, different pressures. Moukoko was already known around the world and tipped for a long career at the top. There was something completely carefree about his style, young Michael Owen-esque. Take a look at his early (and subsequent) goals in the Bundesliga here.

Then life interfered. Moukoko sustained some injuries and struggled to make the Dortmund starting XI. To be fair, he also had some decent competition up front as Erling Haaland had arrived in 2020. Moukoko had a really good spell at the start of the 2022-23 season, after Haaland had joined Manchester City, but sustained an ankle ligament tear and never quite got his starting place back.

These days Moukoko is playing in the Turkish top flight with Corum, on loan from Copenhagen, where he moved in 2025. His switch to the newly promoted Turkish top-flight side was low key with the club welcoming Moukoko to the “family” with a short statement. He is yet to start a game but his cameos off the bench have offered flashes of his quality – most notably marking his home debut with a sharp assist in a 3–0 win over Eyüpspor. His market value is €5m (£4m) reckons transfermarkt.com.

Meanwhile, Hinshelwood has made 67 Premier League appearances and was included on Thomas Tuchel’s 55-man longlist for the 2026 World Cup. A frustrating ankle injury has hampered him at the start of this campaign but his star is rising and he has a market value of €28m (£24m). Not that Brighton are about to sell him.

Neither player chose their path and whether they broke through early. They simply developed at a different pace. Hinshelwood was not ready to play top-flight football at 17; Moukoko was. Did the early exposure have a negative impact on Moukoko? It is impossible to say.

Not that it has been straightforward for Hinshelwood either. It never is. His father, Adam, told Sky this year that “it is definitely not just a straight line”, saying: “There were lots of bumps and ups and downs along the way.” There was one moment when Hinshelwood, then with the under-15s, was set a challenge to play with an older age-group, and that arguably made him as a footballer. “It was a big catalyst for Jack,” Adam said. “He rolled up his sleeves and became a proper footballer.”

Out of our 60 world talents, 24 have gone on to represent their countries. Moukoko stands on two caps, some distance behind players such as Julio Enciso and Gavi. Some have had to swap allegiances to play senior international football, such as Livano Comenencia, who started out with the Netherlands age-group teams but has more than 20 caps for Curaçao and played at this summer’s World Cup.

From our Premier League picks in 2021 astonishingly few players are with the same club. Hinshelwood is one, Liverpool’s Kaide Gordon another, but that is it. The other 18 are playing around the globe, including in the US, Qatar and Hong Kong.

The 20 players have played a total of 145 top-flight games, not a bad tally, but Hinshelwood accounts for almost half of those. Adrian Blake, who was with Watford in 2021, has carved out a very successful career in the Netherlands, having joined Utrecht in 2023. But he too, struggled in the beginning. “It hasn’t been easy and a lots of ups and downs,” he told Football-oranje.com in 2025. “But now I am getting my rewards and showing why I made the right decision by moving here.”

Blake moved to the Netherlands when he was 17. It was a huge gamble for someone so young but he says he chose the Eredivisie “because it is a great league for young players”, offering opportunities that often do not exist in England. “For me it was a no-brainer,” he said.

The 21-year-old has almost his whole career in front of him, as do Moukoko and Hinshelwood – and yet they have experienced so much already. What will the next five years bring?

#995. Thomas Tuchel explains why England are ‘ready’ to end Spain’s unbeaten run

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

England were beaten 3-2 by the world champions in September and now take them on in Madrid

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Thomas Tuchel believes England are “ready” to end Spain’s unbeaten record and prove they can win against the best.

Tuchel’s side head to Madrid on Sunday knowing they must beat Luis de la Fuente’s side to have any chance of topping their group.

While winning the group offers little more than the prospect of a more favourable quarter-final tie in March, the significance of beating the world and European champions on their own patch would go far beyond Nations League standings.

It would be a statement of intent as Tuchel tries to build a side capable of competing with the very best and there is no greater challenge than against a team unbeaten in 43 matches.

“It’s a massive stadium, it’s a massive occasion,” Tuchel said of Sunday’s visit to the Metropolitano Stadium. “It’s a team that has forgotten how to lose, so of course it requires a top performance first of all, and if we can deliver this performance, it will give us a big boost.

“I think we’re there, and I think we’re ready to win on Sunday. I know what it takes, and no one can ever guarantee it, but I think it’s the moment to check how far we are and to push our limit and proof of concept.”

England lost the reverse fixture 3-2 at Wembley in September, but it could have been a different story had Harry Kane scored a penalty to put Tuchel’s men 3-1 up.

There were encouraging signs that night and Tuchel wants to build on it.

“It’s important that we play with the same mindset that we played at home, and attack them and try to make it a physical game, and try to impose our strength,” the German added.

“I think that’s what we want to see. And then you can never predict the result in football, never.

“But it’s important that we show the mindset that you speak of and the spirit, and we will. I’m very confident about that. But honestly, if you look deeply into the matches, even of Spain, they had some crucial ball losses against Croatia.

“They got away with it. They conceded some big, big chances against Croatia and still managed to win the game in the end.

“So no one is unbeatable. We need a top performance, and we’re full of confidence, and we’re getting there.

“I think it’s exactly what we wanted and we feel that we have something to take that we lost the last time.”

Portugal’s former captain hampered a golden generation for too long, but now there is nothing holding them back

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Even in the post-Cristiano Ronaldo era, the shadow of CR7 looms large over Portugal’s national team.

The squad for this month’s Nations League games was framed as ‘Portugal’s first since Ronaldo’s retirement’ by news outlets across the world. Manager Jorge Jesus faced repeated questions about the rift between the pair at last Friday’s press conference. Uncapped youngsters Rodrigo Mora and Gustavo Varela are already being compared to the legendary former captain.

That is to be expected following the international retirement of one of the greatest players of all time. But it also highlights how Portugal players and managers have been unable to break free from the shackles of the Ronaldo soap opera for two decades, often to the detriment of the national side.

Love him or loathe him, you cannot deny that Ronaldo’s numbers are staggering. In an international career that spanned almost a quarter of a century between his debut in August 2003 and his retirement last week, the forward scored 146 goals and won 234 caps, both of which are world records.

He captained Portugal to glory at Euro 2016 - the country’s only major title - and the 2019 and 2025 editions of the Nations League. There were also some brilliant individual performances, including a stunning hat-trick in a 3-3 draw with Spain at World Cup 2018.

At every tournament, Ronaldo dominated the narrative. Until Euro 2016, it was all about his quest for a first international trophy. The defining memory of the final against France was not Eder’s extra-time winner, but Ronaldo effectively appointing himself co-manager by joining head coach Fernando Santos in the technical area and issuing instructions, having earlier been forced off with an injury.

With European glory achieved, it was then all about whether Ronaldo or his great rival Lionel Messi would be the first to win a World Cup. In hindsight, Messi’s triumph at Qatar 2022 with Argentina was the worst thing that could have happened to Portugal.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

That should have been Ronaldo’s last international tournament. He scored just once and was dropped for the last-16 clash with Switzerland after reacting badly to being substituted in the final group match with South Korea, even though Portugal had already qualified. It was the first time since 2008 that Ronaldo had started on the bench at a major tournament.

In came 21-year-old striker Goncalo Ramos, who promptly scored a hat-trick in a 6-1 rout as Portugal produced their best display of the finals. Ronaldo came on as a second-half substitute in the quarter-final against Morocco, but could not prevent a 1-0 defeat.

An exciting new generation started to form in Qatar, with Diogo Costa, Nuno Mendes, Vitinha, Joao Felix, Rafael Leao and Ramos all in their early 20s. It looked like the perfect time for Ronaldo, then aged 37 and with his powers clearly waning, to bow out.

Perhaps he would have retired if Messi had not lifted the trophy, which gave the Argentinian a crucial victory over his rival in the tedious debate over who is the Greatest Of All Time. Instead, Ronaldo embarked on a selfish farewell tour.

Santos was replaced by Roberto Martinez and the new manager sought to appease Ronaldo rather than phase him out. Martinez took an array of attacking talent to Euro 2024 but Ronaldo was the only forward to start every game, despite failing to score a single goal.

The quarter-final against France, which Portugal lost on penalties after a 0-0 draw, highlighted how Ronaldo was now hindering rather than helping his team. The forward was ineffective but played all 120 minutes, while Diogo Jota and Ramos were left on the bench.

Two years on, Portugal arrived at this summer’s World Cup with arguably their strongest-ever squad, featuring back-to-back Champions League victors Mendes, Joao Neves and Vitinha, Premier League Player of the Season Bruno Fernandes and serial winners such as Joao Cancelo, Ruben Dias and Bernardo Silva.

However, Ronaldo again started every game, despite clearly being off the pace. The BBC Sport report from Portugal’s last-32 win over Croatia is telling.

“Their attackers always looked to get the ball to Ronaldo, even when better options were available,” the report says, adding that Portugal “improved” when the 41-year-old was substituted. In the last 16, Ronaldo was again ineffective in a 1-0 defeat by eventual champions Spain, but played 90 minutes.

That is three tournaments in which Ronaldo held Portugal back - three tournaments where a golden generation were forced to fall into line to satisfy their captain’s ego.

Of course, said ego ultimately led to Ronaldo’s international retirement. Offended by new manager Jesus' decision to leave him on the bench for September’s Nations League win in Norway, and then not to start him in the following game, he left the camp. Unsurprisingly, Portugal’s attackers flourished in his absence, with Felix and Ramos each scoring in three of the four matches in that international window.

While Ronaldo will continue to dominate the narrative around the Nations League games against Denmark tomorrow and Wales on Tuesday, Jesus and his players can now look forward to every camp without the constant balancing act of trying to keep their former skipper happy.

It means there is nothing preventing Portugal from being a leading contender at Euro 2028 and World Cup 2030. Neves, Mendes, Vitinha and Fernandes all placed in the top 30 of this year’s Ballon d’Or, with all but the latter aged 26 or under.

Several other players, including Costa, Felix, Leao, Ramos and Pedro Neto are in their mid-20s and already boast plenty of international experience. The older members of the squad, such as Dias, Cancelo, Silva and Fernandes, are all aged 32 or under and have at least one more tournament in them.

It is not the first time Portugal have had this powerful blend of youth, experience and star quality, but now they can harness it properly - free of the burden of having to “get the ball to Ronaldo”.

James Roberts is a freelance sports journalist working for FourFourTwo and other titles. He started his career at the Oxford Mail, where he covered Oxford United home and away, before becoming a sports sub-editor for various national newspapers.

#992. Iconic first image of black hole holds up to scrutiny

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Physicists used an algorithm to combine telescope measurements of a black hole in a different way from the original analysis.Credit: S. Lai, N. Thyagarajan, O. I. Wong and F. Diakogiannis/CSIRO

The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) collaboration wowed the world in 2019 with the first picture ever taken of a black hole’s shadow. Some researchers were unconvinced, arguing that the circular shape seen in that shot was an artefact of the team’s image-reconstruction techniques. Now, an independent group has reanalysed the EHT data, and its results, published on 11 November in Nature — including new images of the black hole — largely corroborate the original findings1.

To image black holes, the international EHT collaboration stitches together data it collects simultaneously from an array of ground-based radio telescopes that stretches across several continents. The reconstruction is extremely challenging, but in principle, the result is an image with the same level of detail, or resolution, that would be achieved with a single radio dish as wide as Earth.

Although blurry, the EHT shot of a supermassive black hole at the centre of the M87 galaxy was consistent with astrophysical models based on Albert Einstein’s general theory of relativity, which first predicted the existence of black holes. The image had a bright ring of roughly the correct radius, given what was known about the size of the black hole, with a darker disk at the centre.

However, starting in 2022, Junichiro Makino, an astrophysicist at Kobe University in Japan, and his collaborators began questioning those conclusions2. By applying one of the data-analysis techniques the EHT collaboration had used, but with slightly different assumptions, Makino’s team obtained a different result. Their image shows a glob of radio emissions rather than a ring.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03642-7

Lai, S., Thyagarajan, N., Wong, O. I. & Diakogiannis, F. Nature https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11241-9 (2026).

Article  Google Scholar

Miyoshi, M., Kato, Y. & Makino, J. Astrophys. J. 933, 36 (2022).
